## Review


- Independent Sample $t$-tests let us compare the means of two different groups
- One way ANOVA lets us compare the means of more than two different groups
- Factorial ANOVA lets us compare the means of more than two crossed factors

Put another way

- Independent Sample $t$-tests let us test one between subjects factor with exactly two levels
- One way ANOVA lets us test one between subjects factor with more than two levels
- Factorial ANOVA lets us test more than one between subjects factor

## Between vs. Within 

Examples of between subjects factors

- Randomizing participants into **exactly one** experimental condition
- Mutually exclusive demographic categories at a given time point
- Comparing students between different sections of the same course

Examples of within subjects factors

- Having all participants go through all experimental conditions in a random order
- Measurements from the same person collected at various time points
- Comparing a group of students who each took the same courses

## Assumption Violations

Which of our assumptions do within subjects designs violate?

- [Independence of observations]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}


Where have we seen a method for handling this violation already?

- [Paired sample $t$-test]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
  - [We simplified things by using a **difference** score so we only had one variable instead of two dependent variables]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
    - [When we have more than two variables, this solution will no longer work]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
    

## Stroop Effect


::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

**Traditional task**: 

<div style="text-align: center;">
[**BLUE**]{style="color: #984EA3;"} &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; [**GREEN**]{style="color: #FF7F00;"} &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; [**RED**]{style="color: #377EB8;"} &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; [**ORANGE**]{style="color: #4DAF4A;"}
</div>

- Difficult to correctly identify the text color of each word

**Idea**: maybe the Stroop effect has to do with contingency rather than congruency

- i.e., Stroop task is hard because we have learned the correspondence between the word "blue" and the color "blue"
- To test this hypothesis, manipulate contingencies between colors and neutral words

<div style="text-align: center;">
[**MEET**]{style="color: #984EA3;"} &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; [**LOOP**]{style="color: #FF7F00;"} &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; [**CALL**]{style="color: #E41A1C;"} &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; [**MEET**]{style="color: #984EA3;"}



[**MEET**]{style="color: #984EA3;"} &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; [**MEET**]{style="color: #984EA3;"} &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; [**SLID**]{style="color: #377EB8;"} &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; [**CALL**]{style="color: #4DAF4A;"}


[**FINS**]{style="color: #377EB8;"} &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; [**MEET**]{style="color: #E41A1C;"} &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; [**LOOP**]{style="color: #4DAF4A;"} &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; [**FINS**]{style="color: #FF7F00;"}
</div>

According to the contingency hypothesis, it should be difficult to correctly indicate "red" for [**MEET**]{style="color: #E41A1C;"}

::: 

## Stroop Replication

::: {style="font-size: 0.6em;"}

**Original study**: Schmidt, J. R., & Besner, D. (2008). The Stroop effect: Why proportion congruent has nothing to do with congruency and everything to do with contingency. *Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning Memory, and Cognition*, *34*, 514--523.
  
**OSF link**: [https://osf.io/x5b6d](https://osf.io/x5b6d)

:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

**Study design**:

* 432 trials, including 6 blocks of 72 trials, 6 words repeated 12 times per block
* Each subject exposed to each type of trial
* Subjects forced to respond quickly
  
**IV**: Contingency level: high, medium, low

**DV**: Proportion of trials where color was identified incorrectly

**Key finding to replicate**: Low contingency trials generate higher performance errors than medium contingency trials

:::


## The Structural Model

**Simplest model**: 

$$y_{ij} = \mu + \pi_i + \tau_j + \epsilon_{ij}$$

- $\mu$: grand mean (overall average score)
- $\pi_{i}$: person's $i$'s deviation from the average person
- $\tau_{j}$: treatment $j$'s deviation from the average treatment mean
- $\epsilon_{ij}$: error associated with person $i$ and treatment $j$


## With Interaction

$$y_{ij} = \mu + \pi_i + \tau_j + (\tau\pi)_{ij} + \epsilon_{ij}$$

- $(\pi\tau)_{ij}$: allows different subjects to change differently over treatments
- Can only be estimated if there are multiple measurements per person + condition combo
- May not be the case in within-subjects designs


## Notation

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

$$y_{ij} = \mu + \pi_i + \tau_j + (\tau\pi)_{ij} + \epsilon_{ij}$$

- $\mu$: overall average proportion of errors
- $\pi_i$: person $i$'s average deviation from the average person mean, across contingency levels
- $\tau_j$: sound condition $j$'s average deviation from the average sound condition mean
- $(\tau\pi)_{ij}$: interaction of person with contingency level
  - If only one observation per cell, no way to distinguish interaction effect and error term
  - There is a $(\tau\pi)_{ij}$ corresponding to every observation, so $\epsilon_{ij} = 0$
  - Can describe every data point exactly

In such cases we instead work with the simpler model.

:::




## One-Way Repeated

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em;"}

Total sum of squares:

$$SST = \sum_i\sum_j(y_{ij} - \bar{y})^2$$


Sum of squares within subjects (treatment effect averaged across individuals):

$$SSA = I\sum_j (\bar{y}_{\bullet j} - \bar{y})^2$$

Sum of squares between subjects (variance in individual differences averaged across treatments):

$$SSS = J\sum_i (\bar{y}_{i\bullet} - \bar{y})^2$$


Sum of squares residual:

$$SSR = SST - SSS - SSA$$

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
* $I$: # subjects, $i = 1, \ldots, I$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
* $J$: # treatment conditions, $j = 1, \ldots, J$
:::

:::

:::

## Refactor!

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em;"}

What if we wanted to test the effect of subject and condition? Then we would have a two-way ANOVA (without interaction) where we treat subjects as a second factor 


Total sum of squares:

$$SST = \sum_i\sum_j(y_{ij} - \bar{y})^2$$



Sum of squares within subjects (treatment effect averaged across individuals):

$$SSA = I\sum_j (\bar{y}_{\bullet j} - \bar{y})^2$$

Sum of squares treating subjects as factor B:

$$SSB = J\sum_i (\bar{y}_{i\bullet} - \bar{y})^2$$

Sum of squares residual:

$$SSR = SST - SSA - SSB$$

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
* $I$: # subjects, $i = 1, \ldots, I$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
* $J$: # treatment conditions, $j = 1, \ldots, J$
:::

:::


:::



## Fixed vs Random

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

**Question:** Do we care if the average error for one participant is different from the others? 

- [We might, but probably not. We're more interested in the effect of **condition** averaged over participants]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
- [But we also need to account for how the participant average effects contribute to our errors]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
- [Another way to think about this is that we need to estimate the **variance** in how people differ even if we aren't testing that factor]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
- [This is sometimes referred to as a "random effect"]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
    - [**Fixed effects:** A complete factor for which we want to compare all levels]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
    - [**Random effects:** A factor where we sample from a population to estimate the variance attributable to that factor, but don't care so much about the specific levels we sample from the population]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}

:::

## Repeated-Measures ANOVA Table

For the Stroop example, $J = 3$ levels of the within-subject IV, and $I = 238$ subjects

Mean squares are calculated as before

For each source of variability, $MS = SS / df$

| Source | $df$ | $SS$ | $MS$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Subject Effect** | 237 | 10.26 | .043 |
| Contingency Level | 2 | .084 | .042 |
| Residual | 474 | .852 | .002 |
| **Total** | 713 | 11.196 | .016 |

## Hypothesis Test

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

The hypothesis test is conducted using the same logic as the between-subjects ANOVA, except for the different error term:

$$F_{obs} = \frac{MSA}{MSR} = \frac{.042}{.002} = 23.42$$


Under $H_0$ (all treatment means equal in the population): 

$$F_{obs} \sim F(dfA, dfR)$$

Like other ANOVA tests, compare $F_{obs}$ to the $F$ distribution

- numerator $df$ = $dfA$ = # within-subject treatment conditions - 1
- denominator $df$ = $dfR$ = (# within-subject treatment conditions - 1)$\times$(# subjects - 1)

:::

## Data Cleaning

The raw data here is in wide format (one column per contingency level)

```{r}
#| echo: true
library(readxl)

dat <- read_xlsx("../../data/Schmidt data.xlsx", 
                 sheet = 2, range = "B20:E257", 
                 col_names = c("Subject", "High", "Medium", "Low"))


head(dat)
```


## Data Lengthening

I am going to pivot it to long format first (multiple rows per person, column indicating contingency level)


```{r}
#| echo: true

dat_long <- dat %>% 
  pivot_longer(High:Low, names_to = "Contingency", values_to = "PropError") %>%
  mutate(Subject = factor(Subject), Contingency = factor(Contingency))

head(dat_long)
```



## In `R` with `aov()`

```{r}
#| echo: true

a1 <- aov(PropError ~ Contingency + Error(Subject / Contingency),
            dat_long)

summary(a1)
```


`Error(Subject / Contingency)` indicates `Contingency` is a within-subjects factor for `Subject`

## In `R` with `ezANOVA()`

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false

library(ez)

ezANOVA(data = dat_long, # dataset
        dv = PropError, # dependent variable
        wid = Subject, # ID's for within-subject variable
        within = Contingency) # repeated-measures IV

```


## Assumptions

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}


1. Independence
    
    - Individuals respond independently of each other
    - Residuals between subjects are independent of each other

2. Covariance structure for the within-subjects factor
  
    - Compound symmetry (stronger)
      - Take the variance-covariance matrix of treatment effects
      - Equal variances: same number on the diagonal of the matrix
      - Equal covariances: same number on the off-diagonals
    - Sphericity (weaker)
      -  Equal variances for all within-subjects variables

Violations of these assumptions can bias the $F$-statistic

:::

## Covariance Structure

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

cov(dat[, -1])

```

```{r}
round(cov(dat[, -1]), 5)
```

**Sphericity**: diagonal elements are equal (in the population)

**Compound symmetry**: sphericity + off-diagonal elements are equal (in the population)


## Mauchly's Test of Sphericity


::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

If sphericity assumption is not met, $F$ is positively biased (Box, 1954)

- Inflated Type I error rate

How far does the covariance matrix deviate from sphericity?

- Mauchly's test is a formal hypothesis test for sphericity
- If sphericity is met, the expected test statistic equals 1
- If $p<.05$, evidence against sphericity
- Mauchly's test only reported for effects with >2 levels because sphericity necessarily holds for variables with 2 levels

Adjustments for positive bias (both available in `ezANOVA`):

- Greenhouse-Geisser
- Huynh-Feldt

Recommended to use adjustments instead of bothering with Mauchly's test

- For reasons comparable to Levene's test in the context of the independent samples $t$-test

:::

## Adjustment for Non-Sphericity


::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

Greenhouse-Geisser (GG) or Huynh-Feldt (HF) adjusted $F$-test:

- Same numerator and denominator $MS$
- Same $F$-statistic
- Adjusted numerator and denominator $df$
- Adjusted $p$-value
- GG and HF use different formulas for $\hat{\epsilon}$ (not shown here)


  $$df_{num, adj}  = \hat{\epsilon} \times df_{num} \\
  df_{den, adj}  = \hat{\epsilon} \times df_{den}$$

- If $\hat{\epsilon} = 1$, adjusted $df$ identical to usual $df$
- If $\hat{\epsilon} > 1$, set $\hat{\epsilon} = 1$ (use original $p$-value)
- If $\hat{\epsilon} > .75$, use Huynh-Feldt, otherwise use Greenhouse-Geisser

::: 

## Adjustment


```{r}
#| echo: true

options(width = 120)

ezANOVA(data = dat_long, # dataset
        dv = PropError, # dependent variable
        wid = Subject, # ID's for within-subject variable
        within = Contingency) # repeated-measures IV
```


- `GGe` is Greenhouse-Geisser $\hat{\epsilon}$
- `HFe` is Hyunh-Feldt $\hat{\epsilon}$
    - Both are $> .75$ so use Hyunh-Feldt, round down to 1

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(readxl)
dat <- read_xlsx("../../data/Schmidt data.xlsx", 
                 sheet = 2, range = "B20:E257", 
                 col_names = c("Subject", "High", "Medium", "Low"))

dat_long <- dat %>% 
  pivot_longer(High:Low, names_to = "Contingency", values_to = "PropError") %>%
  mutate(Subject = factor(Subject), Contingency = factor(Contingency))

dat_long <- dat_long %>% 
  mutate(ContingencyLevel = as.numeric(fct_relevel(Contingency, "Low", "Medium", "High"))) 

dat_long2 <- dat_long %>%
  add_row(Subject = "Average", Contingency = "Low", PropError = .331, ContingencyLevel = 1) %>%
  add_row(Subject = "Average", Contingency = "Medium", PropError = .358, ContingencyLevel = 2) %>%
  add_row(Subject = "Average", Contingency = "High", PropError = .345, ContingencyLevel = 3)

summary(aov(PropError ~ Contingency + Error(Subject), dat_long))
summary(aov(PropError ~ Subject + Contingency, dat_long))
```


```{r}
#| eval: false
library(tidyverse)
library(rstatix)
library(datarium)

# Load dataset and reshape to long format
data("anxiety", package = "datarium")
anxiety_long <- anxiety %>%
  gather(key = "time", value = "score", t1, t2, t3)

# Run Mixed ANOVA
res.aov <- anova_test(
  data = anxiety_long, 
  dv = score, 
  wid = id, 
  between = group, 
  within = time
)

get_anova_table(res.aov)


summary(aov(score ~ group * factor(time) + Error(factor(id)/factor(time)),
          data = anxiety_long))


summary(aov(score ~ group * factor(time) + factor(id), anxiety_long))
```
